Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

gcTMB 0.1.0.9027 (2026-11-27)

  • New variance functions:
    • varExp(), g = exp(t v), as in nlme.
    • varPoly(), a polynomial standard deviation of a chosen degree (default 2), g = 1 + d1 (v - m) + … + dk (v - m)^k, centred at the mean m of v in the data. The likelihood is zero where the polynomial is 0 or below at an observation, and predict() and simulate() give an error where it is 0 or below at new values.
    • varComb(), the product of the g of two or more variance functions, as in nlme, e.g. varComb(varPower(), varExp()) for a standard deviation largest in the middle of growth. Its parameters are named A., B., and so on.
  • korf: the coefficient b2 has the log link by default. It grows with t^(b3 - 1), often to 1e8 or more, where the optimiser stopped with “singular convergence”; on the log scale the fits converge. The coefficients of b2 are now on the log scale, and random effects of b2 act on log b2; link = c(b2 = "identity") gives the old parameterisation.
  • simulate(): a warning about non-finite simulated values suggests the log link of b1 for count models: a simulated random asymptote below zero on the identity scale gives a negative mean.
  • simulate(): the argument random is replaced by re, as random meant the opposite of its meaning in fitted(), residuals() and predict(). re = "new" (default, the old random = TRUE) draws new random effects, re = "fitted" (the old random = FALSE) keeps the fitted ones, and the new re = "none" simulates around the population curve. Scripts with simulate(random = ) must be updated; they now give an error naming the replacement.
  • predict() without newdata failed for times stored as integers (e.g. DAS of the package datasets).

gcTMB 0.1.0.9026 (2026-11-27)

Starting values

  • A coefficient of a covariate in fform without a starting value (NA) is now computed from starting values found separately for each combination of the covariates. Given values are kept, so 0 for the contrasts gives the previous pooled start.
  • start can be a list with the components fixef, VarCorr and sigma, to start the random effects and the residual standard deviation as well.
  • Preece-Baines models have a more robust start.
  • corCAR1(): by default, rho starts where the correlation is 0.2 at the median spacing of the times (before: rho = 0.2).

update() and refit()

  • update() now only sets parameters of a fit: fixef, VarCorr, sigma, corpar and varpar. The argument rho is renamed corpar, and rho is no longer accepted.
  • New refit() fits the model again with other components (e.g. fform, rform, correlation, variance, model, family) and reuses the other arguments. startfrom = "fit" starts from the estimates of the fit where they carry over; startfrom = "data" (default) uses the usual starting values.

Output

  • Print methods show at most 100 rows by default (n in print(), or options(gcTMB.print.max = )), with a note on what was left out and how to get it.
  • Variance components, variance-function parameters and correlation parameters are printed with two decimals.
  • plot(type = "validation2") has one row per grouping factor, in the order of rform, and one column per parameter.
  • timeto() warns about missing or unfitted levels of the grouping variables in newdata, as maxrate() does.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9025 (2026-11-26)

  • maxrate(): rows of newdata with a fitted level of a grouping variable give the curve of that group, with its predicted random effects, as in timeto(); new argument random. Levels that are not in the fit give the population curve with a warning (before, the grouping column was silently ignored).
  • confint() for fits, timeto() and maxrate() gives Wald intervals by default; method = "profile" or "boot" for the others.
  • plot(type = "curves") draws 95% confidence bands of the population curves.
  • viewcurves() shows numbers with the number of decimals of the data.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9024 (2026-11-26)

  • plot(): the outliers observations are drawn in red, with red labels, in the validation graphs.
  • New website article “Exploring observed curves”, with the viewcurves() app running in the browser.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9023 (2026-11-26)

  • viewcurves(): the argument highlight is renamed outliers, as in plot(), and the returned $highlighted is now $outliers.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9022 (2026-11-26)

  • New viewcurves(): a Shiny app to step through the observed curves of a data set, with filters, colours and line types by covariates, and growth rates; or plots of all individuals with the steepest increases and decreases marked (output = "jpeg"). shiny is in Suggests.
  • plot(): type is now "validation1" (residuals, QQ plot and curves), "validation2" (QQ plots of the random effects) or "curves". The observations with the largest absolute residuals (outliers, default 1) are labelled by their individual in models with random effects.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9021 (2026-11-25)

  • New variance functions for the variance argument of gcTMB(): varIdent(), varPower() and varConstPower(), with the arguments and parameterisation of nlme, for the gaussian and lognormal families. The covariate can be a variable of the data, fitted(.) or the growth rate rate(.) of the fitted curve.
  • New varpars(); update(varpar = ); print, summary, coef(), confint(), residuals, simulation, prediction intervals and timeto(residual = TRUE) use the variance function.
  • The default residuals are normalized residuals for the gaussian and lognormal families, and quantile residuals otherwise.
  • New vignette “Variance functions”.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9020 (2026-11-25)

  • New spatial correlation structures corExp() and corGaus(), with an optional nugget and several position variables (form = ~ x + y | group) and euclidean, maximum or manhattan distance.
  • corpars(), coef(), confint(), update(), simulate() and normalized residuals support the new structures.
  • PineHeightDiameter gains the tree positions X and Y.
  • The vignette “Autocorrelation and simulation” is split into “Correlation structures” and “Simulation”.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9019 (2026-11-25)

  • summary() shows the unadjusted Wald test of each coefficient again; partest() gives tests of the differences between curves, adjusted for their number.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9018 (2026-11-24)

  • plot(type = "validation") adds the data with the fitted curves to the page; type = "curves" draws two panels: the individual curves with the data, and the population curves.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9017 (2026-11-24)

  • All column names of the package datasets start with a capital letter (e.g. FabaHeights25$Height, BerkeleyGrowth$Age). The values are unchanged; scripts using the old names must be updated.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9016 (2026-11-24)

  • gcTMBcontrol(onerror = "warning") returns a fit that fails with a warning instead of an error, e.g. in a loop over models; the error is kept in fit$fiterror and reported by print, summary and converged().
  • summary() repeats the convergence warnings of the fit.
  • correlation is now the 7th argument of gcTMB(), after fix, and weights comes after b1type. Calls that pass these arguments by position must be updated.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9015 (2026-11-24)

  • pairwise() is renamed partest(). New argument contrasts: "dunnett" (default, each row of newdata against a reference) or "tukey" (all pairs), with adjust = "single-step".
  • summary() shows estimates and standard errors without tests, and no longer the Pearson dispersion statistic.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9014 (2026-11-24)

  • The shape b3 of the Weibull, gamma and Korf models has the new default link "logm1", log(b3 - 1), which keeps it above 1. Its coefficients are now on that scale; link = c(b3 = "identity") gives the old parameterisation.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9013 (2026-11-22)

  • chapmanrichards is now b4 + b1 (1 - exp(-b2 t))^b3 (Richards 1959), with the rate b2 and the shape b3.
  • The wykoff model is replaced by korf, b4 + b1 exp(b2/((1 - b3) t^(b3 - 1))) (Kuzelka and Marusak 2015). Scripts fitting model = "wykoff" or "chapmanrichards" must be updated.
  • The intercept b4 of both forestry models is fixed by default at the breast height 1.3.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9012 (2026-11-22)

  • New datasets FabaFlowers26 (flowers and pods per plant and date) and FabaNodes26 (flowers and pods per node) from the 2026 field trial.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9011 (2026-11-21)

  • The additive parameter b6 of 0.1.0.9010 is removed again; the models have the parameters b1 to b5.
  • New models: Wykoff (replaced by Korf in 0.1.0.9013), the beta growth function of Yin et al. (2003) as "beta" and "beta_capped", and Preece-Baines model 1 of human growth, whose peak height velocity maxrate() gives in closed form.
  • plot(type = "curves") shows a single numeric covariate on a continuous colour scale.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9010 (2026-11-20)

  • New Chapman-Richards and beta growth models.
  • New datasets BerkeleyGrowth, PineHeightDiameter and SorghumMaize.
  • The x-axis need not be time; the residual plot is labelled with the x variable.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9009 (2026-11-20)

  • No user-visible changes from 0.1.0.9005 (2026-11-19) to 0.1.0.9009: R CMD check fixes on Linux, macOS, Windows and R 4.2, and checks on earlier versions of R.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9004 (2026-11-19)

  • Package website at https://emilskindersoe.github.io/gcTMB/.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9003 (2026-11-18)

  • control = list(restart = TRUE) optimises a fit once more from its estimates when it did not converge, and keeps the better optimum.
  • converged() accepts a restarted fit that the restart improved by less than lltol.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9002 (2026-11-18)

  • Autocorrelated residuals with corAR1() and corCAR1(), whose parameter is called rho.
  • Independent random effects with || in rform.
  • Likelihood ratio tests are named LR in anova().

gcTMB 0.1.0.9001 (2026-11-16)

  • Extractors, criteria(), update(), converged(), and simulation with new data.
  • control option to skip the Hessian and the standard errors for faster fits.
  • Plot types, timeto() and maxrate(), b1 as the maximum growth rate, and pairwise comparisons of curves.

gcTMB 0.1.0.9000 (2026-11-16)

  • First version of gcTMB, developed from drcTMB to fit growth curves only: sigmoid growth models with asymmetry and default truncation, maxrate(), the gaussian, lognormal, binomial, beta-binomial, beta, Poisson and negative binomial families, random effects, and bootstrap intervals.
